lead: A gear train is several gear pairs working one after another. Each pair changes speed and torque by its tooth ratio, and the train multiplies the ratios. An epicyclic train adds an arm, or carrier, that carries a gear round another, so the train has two inputs or one large reduction in a small box. Gear trains drive lathe back gears, car differentials, planetary hubs of excavators and the automatic gearbox of a car.
prereq: You need: speed ratio and centre distance from gear nomenclature.

blocks.text: A simple train has one gear on each shaft. The gears in the middle are idlers: they change the direction of rotation but not the overall ratio. A compound train has at least one shaft carrying two gears fixed together, so large ratios fit in a small space. A reverted train is a compound train whose first and last shafts are in line, as in a lathe back gear or a clock.

For one external pair the driven speed is n<sub>2</sub> = −(z<sub>1</sub>/z<sub>2</sub>) n<sub>1</sub>; the minus sign means the direction reverses. An internal pair keeps the direction. For the whole train:

nlast/nfirst = ± (product of driver teeth)/(product of driven teeth) The ratio is called the train value; its inverse is the speed ratio i. Each external mesh reverses the direction, so count them for the sign.

Example: drivers of 20 and 30 teeth, driven gears of 40 and 60 teeth. Train value = (20 × 30)/(40 × 60) = 1/4, so the output turns at a quarter of the input speed; two external meshes leave the direction unchanged. In a reverted train with one module the centre distances must match: z<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>2</sub> = z<sub>3</sub> + z<sub>4</sub>. With two different modules the condition is m<sub>1</sub>(z<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>2</sub>) = m<sub>2</sub>(z<sub>3</sub> + z<sub>4</sub>).

sections.h3: Epicyclic trains and the tabular method

blocks.text: A simple epicyclic train has a sun S on the central axis, planets P that mesh with the sun and with an internal ring (annulus) R, and an arm or carrier A that holds the planet pins and turns about the central axis. For the planets to fit, zR = zS + 2zP. Several planets share the load; equal spacing needs (zS + zR)/(number of planets) to be a whole number. Some syllabi call this a planetary train.

The train has two degrees of freedom. Fix one member and drive a second, and the third has one definite speed; lock any two members together and the whole train turns as one solid block. The planets both spin and orbit, so the plain tooth ratio does not work. The tabular method handles it in two steps: first hold the arm and turn the sun x revolutions; then turn everything, arm included, by y revolutions. Counter-clockwise is taken as positive.

The planet turns opposite to the sun (external mesh), and the ring turns the same way as the planet (internal mesh). Now put in what is known: a fixed member's total is zero, a driven member's total is its speed. The same result in one line is the relative-speed relation (n<sub>R</sub> − n<sub>A</sub>)/(n<sub>S</sub> − n<sub>A</sub>) = −z<sub>S</sub>/z<sub>R</sub>.

If friction is ignored, the three external torques on the train balance and the power balances: T<sub>S</sub> + T<sub>R</sub> + T<sub>A</sub> = 0 and T<sub>S</sub> n<sub>S</sub> + T<sub>R</sub> n<sub>R</sub> + T<sub>A</sub> n<sub>A</sub> = 0. A fixed member turns at zero speed, so it does no work, but it carries a holding torque. This torque is what a brake band or clutch in an automatic gearbox must hold.

In a car differential the crown wheel drives the cage (the arm) and bevel planets drive the two half shafts. On a straight road the planets do not spin on their pins and both wheels turn at the cage speed; in a turn the inner wheel slows and the outer speeds up, and their average stays equal to the cage speed. In a planetary hub the ring is fixed, the sun is driven and the arm is the output, which gives 3:1 to 10:1 in one stage inside a wheel. A lathe back gear is reverted, not epicyclic. Automatic gearboxes use clutches and brakes to hold different members of planetary sets and so select ratios; the stepped gearboxes of machine tools are taken up in multi-speed gearboxes.

examples.question: An epicyclic train has a sun of 24 teeth, planets of 18 teeth and a ring of 60 teeth. The sun is fixed and the arm turns at 100 rpm counter-clockwise. Find the speed of the ring and of a planet.
steps: Sun fixed: x + y = 0. Arm: y = +100, so x = −100.
Check with the relation: (n<sub>R</sub> − 100)/(0 − 100) = −24/60 gives n<sub>R</sub> − 100 = 40, n<sub>R</sub> = 140 rpm.
examples.answer: The ring turns at 140 rpm and each planet at 233.3 rpm, both counter-clockwise like the arm.

examples.question: The same train is used as a hub reducer: the ring is fixed and the sun is driven at 600 rpm counter-clockwise with 3 kW. Find the arm speed, the planet speed, the speed ratio, the output torque on the arm and the holding torque on the ring.
steps: Arm speed = y = 171.43 rpm counter-clockwise. Speed ratio = 600/171.43 = 3.5 (that is 1 + z<sub>R</sub>/z<sub>S</sub> = 1 + 60/24).
Planet: y − 1.333x = 171.43 − 571.43 = −400 rpm, clockwise. Relative to the arm it spins at −571.4 rpm on its pin.
Power balance with no loss: T<sub>A</sub> × 171.43 = −47.75 × 600, so T<sub>A</sub> = −167.1 N·m: the load holds back the arm with 167.1 N·m, which is 3.5 × 47.75.
Torque balance: T<sub>R</sub> = −(T<sub>S</sub> + T<sub>A</sub>) = −(47.75 − 167.11) = 119.4 N·m. The ring's fixing bolts must hold 119.4 N·m.
examples.answer: Arm 171.4 rpm counter-clockwise, planet 400 rpm clockwise, ratio 3.5, output torque 167.1 N·m, ring holding torque 119.4 N·m.

traps: Using the plain tooth ratio for an epicyclic train. Hold the arm first, then add the arm motion to every member.
Treating every mesh as a reversal. External meshes reverse; a planet and an internal ring turn the same way.
Confusing a planet's absolute speed with its spin on its pin: spin = absolute speed − arm speed.
Saying that fixing two members drives the third. Fixing (or locking) two members locks the whole train; fix one and drive one.
Forgetting the holding torque on the fixed member. It carries torque but no power; the three torques add to zero.

quiz.q: Name the members of a simple epicyclic train.
What is a reverted gear train?
quiz.a: A compound train whose first and last shafts are coaxial; with one module it needs z<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>2</sub> = z<sub>3</sub> + z<sub>4</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is the plain tooth ratio not enough for an epicyclic train?
quiz.a: The planets both spin and orbit. Speeds are first found relative to the arm, then the arm's own speed is added to every member.

quiz.q: Sun 20 teeth, ring 80 teeth; the sun is fixed and the arm turns at 50 rpm. Find the ring speed.
quiz.a: (n<sub>R</sub> − 50)/(0 − 50) = −20/80 = −0.25, so n<sub>R</sub> − 50 = 12.5 and n<sub>R</sub> = 62.5 rpm, in the arm's direction.

quiz.q: Drivers of 20 and 30 teeth, driven gears of 40 and 60 teeth, two external meshes, input 1000 rpm. Find the output speed and direction.
quiz.a: Train value = 600/2400 = 1/4, so the output is 250 rpm, in the same direction as the input.

quiz.q: In the first worked example, fix the ring instead and keep the arm at 100 rpm. Find the sun speed.
quiz.a: (0 − 100)/(n<sub>S</sub> − 100) = −0.4, so n<sub>S</sub> − 100 = 250 and n<sub>S</sub> = 350 rpm, in the arm's direction (ratio 3.5, as in the second example).

quiz.q: Why can a differential let the two wheels turn at different speeds?
quiz.a: Its planet pinions can spin on their pins. One half shaft slows and the other speeds up by the same amount, so their average stays at the cage speed and neither wheel has to slip.

beyond: Not for the exam. Epicyclic sets are the heart of hybrid-car power-split devices, wind-turbine gearboxes and the compact strain-wave and planetary actuators in robot joints. Designers choose tooth numbers for equal planet spacing, then check planet bearing loads and how evenly the planets share the load. Search for Ravigneaux gear set, power-split hybrid transmission and planet load sharing.
